## Review: PR adds `03-node-cli-tool` (Commander.js) — 55 findings triaged

**Operating assumption:** `lib/` is the code under review; `tests/`, `examples/`, `typings/`, and `docs/` get a supporting-material bar. (If this PR is actually *vendoring* upstream Commander rather than authoring it, the only real review question is the vendoring decision and every finding below is moot.)

I verified five findings against the fixture before deciding, because my verdict on 18 of them hinged on file content the scan can't show.

| Decision | Findings | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **Block merge** | 5 | 9% |
| **Warn** (land, file follow-ups) | 13 | 24% |
| **Ignore** | 37 | 67% |

---

## Block merge (5 findings, 2 root causes)

### 1. The parse/spawn seam in `lib/command.js` — `crime_00006`, `crime_00007`, `crime_00011`

Three findings, one root cause. `lib/command.js` is 2180 lines (`severity 0.85`, `confidence 0.95`), and the worst function in it — `_executeSubCommand` at 120 lines (`severity 0.90`) — is also the only place in the module that touches `fs` and `child_process` (`crime_00011`: `fs.existsSync` ×2, `fs.realpathSync`, `lib/command.js:954-976`).

I'm not blocking on line count. I'm blocking because a pure argument parser and a process launcher share one file with one class's mutable state, and that's the seam an agent gets wrong: an edit to option resolution can silently change subcommand path lookup, and neither half can be tested without the other.

**Bounded ask, not a rewrite:** extract `_executeSubCommand` + `findFile` + `incrementNodeInspectorPort` into `lib/execute-subcommand.js`. That removes all filesystem and process access from the parser, and the sync I/O finding becomes a real decision (async lookup) instead of a stylistic one. Blocking is defensible precisely because the remedy is scoped — I'd un-block on this one extraction, leaving the remaining ~1900 lines as a follow-up.

Note `agent_risk` for these is only 0.30–0.36 — *below* three findings I'm ignoring. See the calibration note.

### 2. Duplicated `choices()` validation policy — `crime_00043`, `crime_00044`

`lib/argument.js:99-111` and `lib/option.js:176-188` hold byte-identical `choices` bodies (`confidence 0.95`). This is the cheapest block on the list and the most clearly correct one: it's a **validation policy with two sources of truth in production code**. Add case-insensitive matching, or change the error message, or accept a predicate — an agent fixes one class and ships a library where `.choices()` behaves differently on arguments than on options. `agent_risk 0.22` badly understates this.

Extract one shared `validateChoices(value, choices)` helper.

*Double-count:* `crime_00044` (hash `7f1ce786`, lines 101-109) is the inner block of `crime_00043` (hash `e164bd3a`, lines 99-111). One defect, reported twice.

---

## Warn — land the PR, file follow-ups (13 findings)

| Findings | Call |
|---|---|
| `crime_00008` `parseOptions` (115L), `crime_00030` `_parseCommand` (80L), `crime_00033` `addOption` (69L) | Same file as the block. Real, but 1.1–1.9× threshold and cohesive. Fold into the `command.js` follow-up rather than gating the PR. |
| `crime_00045` `lib/help.js` (462L) | `severity 0.60`. It's one documented, subclassable `Help` class — large but coherent. Warn only. |
| `crime_00031`, `crime_00032` docs drift — 6 dead links in `Readme_zh-CN.md` + `docs/zh-CN/` | The most under-ranked findings in the report (`agent_risk 0.24`). An agent following `./docs/zh-CN/术语表.md` gets nothing, and unlike a style nit this is **provably** broken and takes minutes to fix. Only reason it isn't a block: it's docs, in a non-default locale. |
| `crime_00034`–`crime_00040` (7× `copySettings` weak matchers) | The detector's stated reason is wrong (`toBeTruthy`/`toBeFalsy` on `cmd._hasHelpOption` is a genuine boolean, and each test asserts before *and* after — that's real protection). But there's a defect it didn't name: these assert on **private fields** (`_hasHelpOption`) instead of observable behavior, so an internal rename breaks the suite while a behavior regression slips through. Non-blocking nit, right file. |

---

## Ignore (37 findings)

### The big one: 16 false positives from helper-wrapped assertions — `crime_00012`–`crime_00027`

Every one of these claims "**0 expect/assert calls**." All 16 assert. They route through a shared helper:

- `tests/command.exitOverride.test.js` (8 findings) — `expectCommanderError(caughtErr, 123, 'custom-code', 'custom-message')` at line 84, inside the very block `crime_00012` flags as assertion-free.
- `tests/ts-imports.test.ts` (8 findings) — `checkClass(obj, name)`, which wraps two `expect` calls (`ts-imports.test.ts:9-12`).

`weak_test_signal` counts `expect(`/`assert(` lexically within the test body and doesn't follow single-level helper calls. Extracting a shared assertion helper is *good* test practice — the detector penalizes exactly the suites that did it right. **29% of this entire report is one detector bug**, all at `confidence 0.88`.

### Verified-wrong individually

| Finding | Why ignore |
|---|---|
| `crime_00046` hardcoded `localhost:1234` | It's **in a comment**. `lib/command.js:2152` reads `// e.g. --inspect=localhost:1234`, documenting the regex on line 2151 that parses Node's `--inspect=[host:]port` flag. Not a dev-server URL, not even code. |
| `crime_00009` commented-out code | `search.test.js:13-14` documents the two `childProcess.spawn` signatures the mock asserts against. Explanatory, not disabled. |
| `crime_00028` logic in comments | A dated note with a nodejs.org link explaining why a prior SIGUSR1 workaround was dropped. Rationale is what comments are *for* — that's the opposite of a hidden rule. `confidence 0.65` was appropriately low. |

### Wrong scope class

| Finding | Why ignore |
|---|---|
| `crime_00001` (892L), `crime_00003` (19 booleans) — `typings/index.d.ts` | A hand-written public API declaration file. It's 892 lines because the public surface is. Splitting it churns every consumer's import; renaming `required`/`variadic`/`optional` to `isRequired`/`isVariadic` is a **breaking API change** to ship a naming convention. `crime_00003` is also squarely linter territory. |
| `crime_00002` `"PORT"` scatter | "5 production files" = 4 files in `examples/` and one `typings/index.test-d.ts`. Demo scripts and type tests, not production. Centralizing a constant across standalone examples would defeat their purpose. |
| `crime_00004` duplicate `myParseInt` in `examples/` | Examples are **supposed** to be independently copy-pasteable. Deduplicating them into a shared import makes them worse. |
| `crime_00005` `typings/index.test-d.ts` (481L) | `tsd` type-assertion file; length tracks the API surface. |
| `crime_00029`, `crime_00048`, `crime_00049`, `crime_00051`, `crime_00052` — long `describe` callbacks (206–349L) | This is how Jest suites are written. Splitting adds files and reduces nothing; the detector's own `test callback threshold (200)` concession suggests it half-knows this. |
| `crime_00041`, `crime_00042` variadic weak matchers | `expect(program.options[0].variadic).toBeTruthy()` on an actual boolean. Fine. |

### Threshold noise / not worth a comment

`crime_00047` `lib/option.js` at 327 lines (1.09× threshold), `crime_00010`/`crime_00050` boolean naming on locals and public fields, `crime_00053`–`crime_00055` long documents (CHANGELOG 1244L is append-only by definition; the two Readmes are 1.1×). Of these, `crime_00054` (`Readme.md`, 1130L) is the only one I'd defend as a warn — agents genuinely do load it in fragments.

---

## Calibration note for the crimes team

**The report's ranking is inverted relative to the review outcome.** The top five findings by `agent_risk` — 0.48, 0.46, 0.43, 0.37, 0.37 — are all ignores. Both blocks sit lower, and the cheapest, most clearly correct block (`choices` duplication) ranks **44th of 55** at `agent_risk 0.22`.

The cause is mechanical and checkable: those top five findings (`crime_00001`–`crime_00005`) are **exactly** the five findings in the report carrying `test_gap: 0.75`. Every one is in `typings/` or `examples/`. Meanwhile `lib/command.js` — the actual god file — carries `test_gap: 0`.

That's arguably correct on its own terms (a `.d.ts` and a demo script have no tests; `command.js` is well covered), but the consequence is that `test_gap` supplies most of the `agent_risk` signal for file classes where tests are meaningless, and it floats a type-declaration file above a 2180-line parser. Suggested fix: suppress or heavily discount `test_gap` for scope classes that can't meaningfully be tested (`.d.ts`, `examples/`, type-test files) — `util/scope-class.ts` already knows how to make that call.

Second: `weak_test_signal` should resolve single-level in-file helper calls before reporting "0 expect calls." At `confidence 0.88` with a 16/16 miss rate on this fixture, it's the loudest wrong signal in the report — and it happens to punish the exact refactor the tool recommends elsewhere.
